Task: Develop a complete lesson plan for teaching probability to high-school students.

High-School Mathematics Lesson Plan  
Topic: Introduction to Probability (1 double period—90 minutes total)

1. Lesson Overview  
   Students learn fundamental probability concepts, distinguish theoretical vs. experimental probability, and apply rules for simple and compound events using real-life contexts (dice, cards, spinners). The lesson blends direct instruction, hands-on experimentation, discussion, and technology to address diverse learning styles.

2. Standards Alignment  
• Common Core HS-S.MD.A.1, A.3—Understand and calculate probabilities of events.  
• NGSS Science & Engineering Practice: Analyzing & Interpreting Data.  
• Mathematical Practice (CCSS): MP1, MP2, MP4, MP5, MP6.

3. Learning Objectives (SWBAT = Students Will Be Able To)  
SWBAT 1: Define probability, outcome, sample space, event.  
SWBAT 2: Compute theoretical probability of a simple event (P = favorable outcomes ⁄ total outcomes).  
SWBAT 3: Conduct an experiment, record relative frequency, and compare experimental to theoretical probability.  
SWBAT 4: Use addition rule for mutually exclusive events and multiplication rule for independent events.  
SWBAT 5: Evaluate probabilities in real-world contexts and justify reasoning.

4. Prerequisite Knowledge  
• Fractions, ratios, and percentages.  
• Basic set notation and operations (union, intersection not required but helpful).

5. Materials & Technology  
• One six-sided die per pair.  
• Decks of playing cards (one per group).  
• Coins, spinners or online spinner simulation.  
• Chart paper / whiteboard & markers.  
• Student handouts (guided notes, practice problems, exit ticket).  
• Graphing calculators or Chromebook/tablet with probability simulation applet (e.g., GeoGebra, Desmos).  
• Projector/slides.

6. Time & Activity Sequence (90 min)  
A. Warm-Up (10 min)  
   – Slide shows three everyday questions: “Will it rain today?”, “Is my bus on time?”, “What’s the chance of drawing an ace?”  
   – Students write quick estimates; class brainstorms what “chance” means.  
   – Transition: “Today we’ll formalize this intuitive idea as probability.”

B. Direct Instruction: Core Concepts (15 min)  
   – Teacher mini-lecture with guided notes: definitions (trial, outcome, sample space, event, probability).  
   – Formula P(E) = n(E)/n(S); show simple examples (coin, die).  
   – Emphasize 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 and probability as long-run relative frequency.

C. Exploration 1: Dice Simulation (20 min)  
   – Students in pairs roll a die 30 times, tally results, compute relative frequencies, and graph bar chart.  
   – Compare class aggregate data to theoretical 1/6. Discuss variability and “law of large numbers.”  
   – Extension question: Predict after 10,000 rolls (connect to computer simulation shown by teacher).

D. Direct Instruction: Compound Events (10 min)  
   – Introduce addition rule for mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B).  
   – Demonstrate with die (P(roll even) = P(2)+P(4)+P(6)).  
   – Introduce independent events multiplication: P(A and B)=P(A)·P(B). Example: coin then die, probability of heads and a 5.

E. Exploration 2: Cards & Probability Stations (25 min)  
   Station 1—Cards: Probability of drawing a heart; of a red card then a king without replacement (dependent events).  
   Station 2—Spinner: Theoretical vs. experimental with unequal sectors.  
   Station 3—Technology: Students use simulation applet for flipping 100, 1,000, 10,000 coins; record convergence.  
   Each group rotates every 8 min; fill in handout.

F. Synthesis & Discussion (5 min)  
   – Groups share surprising findings.  
   – Teacher highlights key rules, common misconceptions (e.g., gambler’s fallacy).

G. Assessment & Closure (5 min)  
   – Exit Ticket: 1) Define sample space. 2) Bag has 3 red, 2 blue marbles; probability of drawing blue? 3) Are events rolling a 4 on a die and drawing an ace independent? Explain.  
   – Collect for formative assessment.

7. Differentiation  
• Visual aids (Venn diagrams, tree diagrams).  
• Concrete manipulatives for tactile learners.  
• Challenge problems (conditional probability) for advanced students.  
• Sentence frames for ELLs (“The probability of ___ is ___ because ___.”).

8. Homework  
Worksheet: 10 problems—mix of simple and compound events; one reflection question comparing experimental vs. theoretical probability.

9. Assessment Plan  
Formative: Warm-up responses, observation during stations, exit ticket.  
Summative (later): Quiz on probability rules; project (design a carnival game, calculate fair odds).

10. Reflection (for teacher after lesson)  
• What misconceptions persisted (e.g., equiprobability bias)?  
• Did students appropriately apply multiplication rule to independent events?  
• Were station times adequate? Adjust for next lesson.
